title: The most important muscle for breathing is a dome under your lungs

cover.alt: A black-and-white MRI slice through a chest: the heart in the middle, dark lungs on each side and the grey liver below the dome of the diaphragm.
cover.credit: Biomedizinische NMR Forschungs GmbH · CC BY-SA 3.0

body: The **diaphragm** is a sheet of skeletal muscle that separates your chest, with the heart and lungs, from your abdomen. When you breathe in, it contracts and moves down, which enlarges the chest, lowers the pressure inside and lets the lungs fill with air. Your large liver rests just beneath its right half, and in the clip you can watch it slide down during a deep breath. The diaphragm works both on autopilot and under your control.

slides.alt: Real-time MRI of a person's chest: the heart beats in the middle, and during one deep breath the dark lungs grow taller as the diaphragm and the liver below it move down.
slides.caption: Real-time MRI of a chest: the heart beats in the middle. During one deep breath the dark lungs expand as the diaphragm, and the liver under it, move down.

slides.prompt: Is your diaphragm under your control, or does it run on autopilot?
slides.detail: It is skeletal muscle, the kind you can command, and you can hold your breath. But it is also under involuntary control, so it keeps you breathing without a thought.

slides.heading: It does more than breathe
items: Squeezes the belly to help push out vomit, faeces and urine
Helps stop stomach acid flowing back up

slides.question: Which nerve mainly controls the diaphragm?
slides.explanation: The phrenic nerve, which is formed from three nerves in the neck: C3, C4 and C5.
